publisher: TU Delft — BSc Computer Science and Engineering, Matching & Selection
claim: Computer Science & Engineering is numerus fixus with 590 places for 2027-2028, 345 of them in the English track. Applications close 15 January 2027. A Matching phase must be completed to receive a ranking number but does not affect it; selection tests mathematics and systematic reasoning, and the test score only decides which of three lottery categories an applicant is drawn from.
excerpt: The Computer Science & Engineering bachelor’s programme at TU Delft has a Matching & Selection (Numerus Fixus) procedure. This means that only a limited number of spots are available, and all candidates are selected via the Matching & Selection procedure. We can welcome 590 new bachelor students for the academic year 2027-2028. There are 345 spots reserved for the English track and 245 spots for the Bilingual track (Dutch-English). The application opens in October 2026 and closes on 15 January 2027. [...] Students with a foreign diploma are solely admissible for the English track, unless they fulfil the Dutch language requirements of the Bilingual track. [...] You have to complete the Matching elements in order to receive a ranking number, but they do not influence your place in the ranking. For the selection part all candidates will be tested on two selection criteria: Mathematics; Systematic Reasoning & Logical Thinking. [...] Your final ranking number is a unique number and is assigned completely random from the drawn numbers in the category in which you were placed.
interpretation: Three things here matter to a student and none of them is a grade. The English track is the only one open to a foreign diploma, so the number that governs is 345 rather than 590. The Matching phase is compulsory and carries no weight, which is the opposite of what its name suggests to anyone who has met a British admissions test. And the selection is not a ranking of scores: the score chooses a lottery category and the place within it is drawn at random, so a very strong candidate in category 1 can still lose to chance.

[...] Only the full IB Diploma is accepted. IB certificates and IB Career-related programme are not accepted. [...] Mathematics requirement: Mathematics Analysis & Approaches SL minimum grade 5 OR Mathematics Analysis & Approaches HL minimum grade 4 OR Mathematics Applications & Interpretation HL minimum grade 5 [...] If you do not meet any of the above requirements, you must take a mathematics proficiency exam. [...] Selection points: You will be granted selection points if you have a total of 33 points based on the 6 exam subjects (excluding TOK and EE) or higher. If your grades are below this, you will not earn selection points for your final ranking. [...] Your total IB points will be calculated based on the grades of your penultimate year (the year before your final year). Predicted grades are not used for the evaluation.
interpretation: The 33-point line is the reason this repository keeps Requirements and Selection Factors apart. It is not an entry requirement: an applicant below 33 is still eligible and their application is still valid, they simply earn no selection points and are therefore not ranked. Recorded as mandatory: false for that reason. Recording it as a requirement would tell a 32-point student they cannot apply, which is false; recording it nowhere would tell them they have a chance, which is worse. Note also that RSM evaluates penultimate-year grades and explicitly does not use predicted grades — for an IB student this means the grades that decide a Rotterdam place were earned in the first year of the Diploma.

[...] Creative Business — STAGE A: 50% [application letter, resume, study skills test, previous knowledge test]; Stage B: 50% [interview]. [...] Applied Data Science & Artificial Intelligence — 20% Motivation; 20% Suitability and communication skills; 60% Mathematics test + experience and presentation. Scoring and selection: >70% = Selected; 60-70% = Waiting list; <60% = Not selected.
interpretation: The deadline is the thing to read twice. The national rule is that a capped programme closes on 15 January; BUas states that its own bachelor programmes with selection close in Studielink on 1 May. Both are official and they are not describing the same instrument — a hogeschool selection at the gate is not the same legal creature as a university numerus fixus — but this pass did not establish which article of the WHW BUas is applying, so the divergence is recorded rather than resolved, and the dates recorded on the route are BUas's own because BUas owns its own procedure. Note also what is being selected on: a video message, a portfolio, an interview, a study-skills questionnaire. Grades appear nowhere except through the mathematics test for Applied Data Science. An IB student who assumes Dutch selection means grades will prepare for the wrong thing.

excerpt: International Business is a numerus fixus programme with selection by the educational institution. This means that you go through a selection process after applying. Due to the limited number of places we cannot offer a place to every applicant who meets the admission requirements. [...] Deadline for all applicants to: apply via Studielink; complete all admission tasks [...] in the MyApplication portal. [15 January, 23:59 CET] [...] Outcome selection procedure and publication ranking number [15 April, 23:59 CET] [...] Their assessment is based on your: International Classroom Essay (33%); Curriculum vitae + supporting documents (33%); Grades of your penultimate year of secondary school (33%). This means that you will not be able to start this bachelor's programme. [...] This decision will also be valid for the bachelor's programme in Economics and Business Economics, since the International Classroom requirement is the same for both programmes.
interpretation: The International Classroom requirement is the hardest thing in this pass to file. It is not an entry requirement — it is judged on an essay, after application, by a committee — and it is not purely a ranking factor either, because failing it removes you from the ranking rather than lowering you in it. It is recorded as a Selection Factor because that is where the model puts anything that is assessed rather than held, and the note says plainly what failing it costs. Note too that it is decided once for both International Business and Economics and Business Economics, so applying to the second as a fallback against the first does not work.

claim: University College Maastricht has 250 places, a two-round selective admission of document review then an online interview in English, and deadlines of 1 February 2027 for non-EU/EEA applicants and 1 April 2027 for EU/EEA and Swiss applicants. Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis. First-year students must earn 45 of 60 ECTS or be excluded from the programme for six years.
excerpt: At UCM, we are looking for highly motivated students with a genuine passion for academics. To find the right match between your academic interests and what UCM offers, we use a selective admissions process. Each year, we have 250 places available for new students. [...] 1 February 2027, 23:59 CET — Deadline for applicants with a non-EU/EEA nationality [...] 1 April 2027, 23:59 CET — Deadline for applicants with an EU/EEA or Swiss nationality [...] At UCM, we review applications on a rolling basis, so you can apply at any time up until the deadline. [...] First round: The Board of Admissions will review your application documents and let you know by email if you have been selected for an interview. Second round: If selected, you will be invited for an online interview in English with a UCM academic staff member. The interview takes about 30-45 minutes and focuses on your academic plans and how you see your education at UCM supporting these goals. [...] in your first year of the programme, you must obtain a minimum of 45 out of 60 ECTS credits.
interpretation: Neither Dutch deadline applies here. UCM is selective but not numerus fixus, so it sets its own dates — 1 February or 1 April depending on nationality, both earlier than the national 1 May and later than the numerus fixus 15 January. A student who has learned 'the Dutch deadlines are 15 January and 1 May' will get this wrong in either direction. The Binding Study Advice is recorded because it is the kind of thing nobody reads until it applies to them: 45 of 60 credits in year one, and failing it closes all three Maastricht liberal-arts programmes for six years.

excerpt: With the International Baccalaureate (IB) diploma, you will probably be admissible to a bachelor's programme at the University of Twente. This depends on the subjects and their corresponding levels you have achieved. [...] In general, there is no minimum IB grade requirement. [...] The 'Career-related Certificate of the International Baccalaureate' is not directly admissible to the University of Twente. [...] These admission requirements are valid for the September 2026 intake. The requirements are announced in October for the following September intake moment. The University of Twente therefore cannot provide any information regarding admission requirements for future intake moments that are not yet open for applications. [...] English Language A: Literature – Standard Level or Higher Level - Grade ≥ 4; English Language A: Language and Literature – Standard Level or Higher Level - Grade ≥ 4; English Language B – Standard Level - Grade ≥ 6; English Language B – Higher Level - Grade ≥ 5. [...] A high score in a Standard Level (SL) subject cannot replace the same subject at Higher Level (HL) when the subject on HL is required for admission.
interpretation: Twente is the honest edge of the ADR 0002 question. Its central IB page is written entirely in IB terms — named IB subjects, IB levels, IB grades — and needs no translation. Its programme pages are not consistent with each other: Advanced Technology names IB subjects, Technical Computer Science asks instead for mathematics 'comparable to a pre-university level, such as VWO Wiskunde B', and Creative Technology names no subject at all. So one university does all three things at once, and the reason this still does not amount to a case for a Recognition Scheme is that nobody publishes the table a scheme would need: Twente does not say what IB mathematics counts as Wiskunde B, and Nuffic publishes no subject equivalence either. A scheme here could only be written by inventing it.

interpretation: This is the one requirement found in the Netherlands that is genuinely written on a local scale rather than in IB terms, and it is recorded as published rather than translated into an IB subject nobody gave us. ADR 0002 offers two shapes for a requirement — IB terms, or a local scale named by a Recognition Scheme — and this is a third: a comparison to a local qualification for which no authority publishes an equivalence. Neither Twente nor Nuffic says what IB mathematics counts as VWO Wiskunde B. A Recognition Scheme could therefore only be invented, and the repository's own guard refuses a local-scale requirement whose scale nothing defines, so the requirement is recorded as kind 'other' with the official wording kept whole. The consequence is deliberate: the engine reports that it cannot check this and sends the student to the official page. A requirement we cannot check is better data than a requirement we quietly answered for them.
